title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction: This page continues the introduction of E740 (presented 8 March 1779, published 1813). It sets up a variational problem for curves in space. Paragraph 2 (end): if the integral formula involves three variables x, y, z, it has a definite value only when two of them are functions of the third. One must therefore find both relations y(x) and z(x). Read as coordinates, these give a curve that does not lie in one plane, and two equations are needed to determine it. Paragraph 3: take three mutually perpendicular axes OA, OB, OC, with OA and OB in the plane of the drawing and OC perpendicular to it (Tab. I, Fig. 1). A point Z of the curve has coordinates OX = x, XY = y, YZ = z. For each abscissa x both ordinates y and z must be given, so two equations are needed. The equation between x and y describes the projection of the curve on the plane AOB. The equation between x and z, after drawing XV parallel and equal to YZ, describes the projection on the plane AOC. The next page adds that the projection on BOC follows from these two. In modern terms the curve is the graph x -> (y(x), z(x)) in R^3, given by two cylinder projections, and the problem is to make ∫V dx extremal over such curves. This is the setup for the Euler–Lagrange system with two unknown functions, which comes on the following pages.
errors: None mathematically. The page uses 'axos' for 'axes'; this is either a printing slip or Euler's own form.

ideas.what: A space curve represented by two equations y = y(x), z = z(x), i.e. by its projections on two coordinate planes; the third projection then follows.
ideas.modern_name: Graph or parametrization of a space curve by projections onto coordinate planes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Clairaut (Recherches sur les courbes à double courbure, 1731); Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, Vol. II, Appendix (1748)
ideas.where_published: Introductio in analysin infinitorum II, Appendix (E102)

ideas.what: Extremizing an integral that depends on two unknown functions of one variable requires two determining relations, one equation for each function.
ideas.modern_name: Variational problem with several dependent variables (Euler–Lagrange system)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (δ-method, 1760–62); Euler also handled multiple unknown functions in the Methodus inveniendi (1744) and the Institutiones calculi integralis III supplement
ideas.where_published: Lagrange, Misc. Taurinensia 1760–61; Euler, E65 and related papers

deep.surprise_reason: This is standard introductory setup: coordinates and projections of a space curve, and the observation that two unknown functions need two equations. All of it was well established by 1779 (Clairaut, Euler's Introductio, Lagrange). Nothing on the page is new or overlooked.
transcription_corrections: 'Quodsi jam z fuerit punctum' should read 'Quodsi jam Z fuerit punctum' (the point Z, capital letter), not the variable z.
'axos' is as printed (presumably for 'axes'); leave it but note it.
